reviews.review: My son and my grandkids bought Deep Rock Galactic for me.  Once I become familiar with the play, it became my favorite game.  It is so much fun to fight the big bugs on a team with them. Connecting with them this way is so precious. Also, this is the most entertaining way to maintain brain plasticity that I've discovered so far.

-No microtransactions
-No gambling
-No predatory matchmaking (it's all peer-to-peer)
-No psychological manipulation designed to get you to spend
-No obscene "you will own nothing and be happy" EULA

What more can you ask for?

It's not a game made by ultra-wealthy executives hunting for whales to feed their shareholders. It's a game made with passion. Passion which was used to create a very compelling game, not a bullshіt in-game store, or bullshіt legalese terms and conditions, or bullshіt telemetry, or bullshіt psychological tricks. While Deep Rock Galactic stands out as unique for not being overwrought with such things, it's a wonderful game in its own right, which I'm sure the loads of other positive reviews will do a better job at highlighting what makes it so wonderful.

One of the best games I was ever given to play, it's worth your time.
Absolutely amazing anti-FOMO features I've ever seen in games, should be the standard for all devs.

Everything about this game is just one word: perfect. The community, the devs, the weapons and gadgets we get for our dwarves, the mods and the modding comunity, the soundtracks, the atmosphere, the  bug variety it’s all amazing. What really makes the game endlessly replayable are not just the weapons, upgrades, and overclocks, but also the players themselves. Every match feels different, not only because of the loadouts, but because of the absolute chaos your teammates bring: 

The Drillers who carry a brick of C4 and blow up literally everything including teammates when they feel threatened. most of the time themselves.

The maniacs who turn every Liquid Morkite mission into a rollercoaster ride.

The rookies who join high difficulty lobbies with sky-high confidence, only to fall down every five seconds, forcing you to babysit them like a full-time nanny.

And countless other weird, wonderful personalities that make each run unpredictable.

On the weapons side, every build makes you feel like you are playing a new game. I’ve got almost 3000 hours in this game, and I’m still finding new combinations. Wanna be a vampire? Grab the Cryo Cannon, get thge Vampire perk, and freeze bugs solid while sucking the life out of them. They can’t move, they can’t fight back, you just heal yourself by powerdrilling them like a maniac while they stand there, helplessly.
Wanna be a maniac ice wizard instead? Throw on the Ice Spear overclock and start throwing massive ice spikes to everything that moves and deal ♥♥♥♥ ton of damage. And to everyone who says “Scout is just support, can’t deal with crowds” nah uh . Stick Cryo Minelets on zhukov, pair it with Aggressive Venting for the Plasma Carbine, and suddenly you’re outkilling Engineers. Speaking of Engineers, you don’t even need to move to deal with those ugly aracnids: cover the ground around you with platforms, electrify them with Micro Conductor overclock (one of the stubby smgs overclock), drop some turrets, unleash your flying buttplugs (yeah, those little shredder guys), and watch the bugs fry while you just sip your beer.
As Gunner, equip Cluster Charge, find yourself a jetboot if you are lucky, and boom you’re basically a B-52 bomber dropping hundreds of tiny clusters on everything below. Pure chaos. Absolute joy.

The caves? Beautiful. Genuinely gorgeous. But after enough hours like a thousand, you kinda start predicting the formations, which is my only tiny complaint. I’d love to see new ones in the next updates but still they’re hypnotic. Every cave feels magical. Go in not just to kill bugs, but to explore and you’ll see what I mean.

The music and atmosphere? straight up brainwashes you. Like, you’re not just playing a game anymore you’re living in Hoxxes and i mean it i would sell my soul to a space mining company like drg.

The community? Honestly feels like we’re all sharing the same single brain cell. And thats perfect. You’ll have some of the dumbest and funniest moments of your life.

And the true heart of the game: the Space Rig.
Dance until you pass out from drinking with buddies. Play Prop Hunt (yes, there’s literally a beer that lets you do that). Kick barrels around, play Jetty Boot, the in-game Flappy Bird game, Or my personal favorite: fill your afk teammate’s quarters with barrels until they come back to find a surprise barrel-apocalypse waiting for them.
I swear I’ve spent at least 500–600 hours in the Rig alone. Which other game lets you have that much fun without even actually playing the game?

Long story short: every cent you spend on this game is worth it. You’re gonna have fun 100%.

And finally: ROCK AND STONE, YOU BEAUTIFUL DWARFES!

As a middle-aged woman with bills, responsibilities, and limited gaming time, I love Deep Rock Galactic because it respects my time: clear missions, controlled chaos, satisfying teamwork, and a proper sense of completion. Even if someone gets distracted by an interesting flying bug (THAT'S ME), the team can usually still get the job done. No vague life-purpose crisis. No endless open-world wandering pretending to be freedom. Just a contained mission with a finish line.

And my tired brain likes closure....

[h3]Thousand Hour Review[/h3]
If there’s a game that I gotta leave a review for, it’s this one. A lot of passion and care is put into this game, and that’s something hard to find in a lot of mainstream games nowadays. Everything from the very cooperative gameplay and the engagingly complex mission designs, to the phenomenal soundtrack and immersive sound design, to the characters of the game and their many quirky voice lines, to the smaller details like the many neat things found in our hub area, the Space Rig, the charming low-poly artstyle, to even the Miner’s Manual. It's the help section of the game, and its design is crafted in such a way reminiscent of physical game manuals, covering basically everything you need to know about the game with stylized instructions. Art direction and details aside though, this game embodies the very definition of fun.

The entire game itself emphasizes teamplay and cooperation, and builds upon it, especially with the many voicelines mentioning to leave no dwarf behind, and it honestly has the most wholesome community that I’ve ever seen, especially coming from other FPS games that are just about guaranteed to carry a high-strung, toxic crowd from within those playerbases. In my time playing this game, I’ve barely come across any toxic experiences, enough to count on one hand. A majority of the people are willing to help and cooperate with each other, like asking if everyone’s ready to progress the objective through typing “r” in the chat. Even failing missions is barely a big deal. Part of the fun in multiplayer is just sharing a beer and celebrating with your teammates at the Abyss Bar in the Space Rig! There are difficulties tailored for everyone, and there are options to host a lobby yourself, join others’ lobbies, set a friends’ only lobby, or to go completely solo, and you won’t be alone either! You’ll have the option to take an All-Purpose Drone, nicknamed Bosco, with you on your expedition. And he is quite literally all-purpose, as Bosco can do half of the work for you. Just ping an object, or objective, and he can mine, carry items, shine light, shoot enemies, revive, build and repair objectives, guard objectives, and so much more!

As you start a mission and send yourself into the depths of Hoxxes, you’ll find yourself in the many different and also very wonderfully crafted biomes that you’ll perform these missions in. Having many biomes available means you aren’t just surrounded by stone, but you can find yourself surrounded by ice, grass, sand, wood, or other organic material. And there’s even more than just enemies and minerals to expect too, as there is also plant life, fauna, and varying hazards present depending on where you are conducting your missions. The maps themselves are randomly generated and the entirety of the map is destructible, allowing you to shape the map however you’d like. The caverns are your sandbox.

Progression-wise, after every mission you complete, you’ll take home some credits, XP, and any acquired minerals. The minerals you find can be used at the loadout terminals to mod and upgrade your gear or at the shop to purchase something new for your wardrobe. And to those who love character creation or game fashion, there's a ton of customization available, leaving room for tons of unique combinations! There is a specific terminal to the left of the Drop Pod however, the Assignment terminal. It contains objectives where you must complete a set of missions to work towards the rewards offered by it. Rewards include weapons, cosmetics, materials, and unlocking promotions for the dwarves. 

Promotions are where the progression truly starts. As you bring any of the dwarves up to level 25, you’ll have an opportunity to complete a promotion assignment for that class, unlocking the ability to promote your dwarf. The promotions act as a prestige system for the game. Alongside the promotions, you’ll unlock access to the Forge, Core Hunts, Deep Dives, Overclocks, and some other things, serving as a kind of endgame content. As you continue on playing the game, I highly recommend getting to this point as Overclocks drastically change how each class’ weapons work, allowing for lots of different playstyles to keep the game feeling fun and fresh.

As for the monetization of this game, the game only offers DLCs that are purely cosmetic and does not give any form of progression advancements. There is no “premium currency” for the game. With that, the game also includes its own battle pass system known as the Performance Pass. Just wait though! Even if you're tired of hearing about battle passes, don't let that turn you away! The Performance Pass system is completely free and does not require any real world purchases for any kind of "premium tier" cosmetics. Its structure is comprised of the standard tiered system but is also paired alongside a cosmetic tree. The Performance Passes are also not timegated in any way, and you are free to progress any Performance Passes from previous seasons as well, making all cosmetics and its contents obtainable as part of the natural progression of the game.

On the technical side of things, the game runs fairly well and most notably, it barely takes up any storage space, as the game’s file size is only 3 GB! That kind of file size is basically unheard of today with many AAA games taking upwards of 70+ GB on your drives, save for some older games or indie titles. If you are also one that enjoys modding games, the game includes official built-in modding support through Mod.io, allowing for client-sided ‘Verified’ mods, the gameplay-enhancing ‘Approved’ mods, and the ‘Sandbox’ mods. All mods can be changed on the splash screen menu before you enter the game, no need to dig into your file explorer to edit the mods. Because there is modding support, you may even find modded servers when looking through the server list. And just in case that you accidentally joined a modded server and had undesired changes made in your progression, the game also includes a save menu within the options tab, allowing you to revert to a previous cloud save.

This is an absurdly long review, yes, but again I just cannot recommend this game enough as there is just so much to like about it. You can also read the opinions from the many other reviewers around and see that there’s a good reason why this is among the top rated games on Steam. The game goes on sale constantly and is easily a great buy for your library. If you do end up getting the game, always be sure to Rock and Stone. See you in the caves.

[b]We Fight, We Mine
For Rock and Stone[/b]

After 84 hours in Deep Rock Galactic, I’ve learned two universal truths: teamwork matters, and someone is always going to press the button too early. Playing this with my kiddos has been an absolute blast — not just because shooting alien bugs is fun, and mining precious gems is lucrative, but because the game quietly teaches cooperation while pretending it’s just about yelling “I NEED AMMO” at full volume. Every mission is different, every cave is a mystery, and every drop feels like a shared “OK, we got this!” moment .. which we absolutely do NOT half of the time, but that's half the fun. And the fully destructible environments are just icing on the cake.

The magic is in the details. Random missions that somehow never feel repetitive. Loadouts that actually force you to rely on each other. Collectible cosmetics that range from “battle-hardened space dwarf” to “what happened in the locker room?” And the Space Rig? A perfect between-mission chaos zone where we drink absurdly well-crafted space beer, gain questionable buffs, dance badly, and laugh when gravity suddenly becomes optional. It’s unapologetically over-the-top, intentionally built, and ridiculous in exactly the right way.

The seasonal objectives and progression are sneakily brilliant. There’s always something to work toward — new cosmetics, upgrades, scrip, and rewards that make you say “one more mission” way more times than you planned. Weapons and equipment steadily evolve, letting you tweak builds, unlock overclocks, and turn your dwarf into a highly specialized bug-destroying professional (or an unhinged explosives enthusiast). It’s rewarding without being grindy, and it gives you a sense of progress and accomplishment without sucking the fun out of it.

Deep Rock Galactic doesn’t just reward skill — it rewards paying attention, backing each other up, and laughing when things go sideways (which they will). It turns cooperation into comedy, chaos into bonding, and random moments into memories. Whether you play with family or friends, this game will quickly reveal who communicates, who panics, and who absolutely should not be trusted with big red buttons.

Dwarves, beer, mining, and guns - what could possibly go wrong? Also, repeatedly moving the M.U.L.E. every five seconds does not make the mission faster, it makes your coworkers tired, and is classified as ‘hostile workplace behavior.’ :D

Rock and Stone!

This is an in-depth comparative review, coming from someone who's been playing since the game went 1.0, and has sunk multiple hundreds of hours into Helldivers 2, Space Marine 2, and Darktide. 

I think that DRG is far more engaging and replayable than any other co-op PVE shooter on the market because of its level-design. Every other game in this genre I can think of has handmade levels. They look stunning but are partially memorized within ~5 runs and on the 20th they don't really have anything to surprise you. The gameplay becomes a matter of knowing how to use specific kiting routes, when you can count on pick-ups spawning, and where you may encounter minibosses. 

Each mission in DRG is entirely procedural, if you do the same mission twice, you will have an entirely different experience each time. The gameplay is not the aforementioned memory-exercise. You're improvising everything: how do I defend this position when it's on a cliffside, the middle of a tunnel, or a wide-open expanse? how do I evade this horde? There is NOTHING like the rush you get when a swarm spawns and you (and your teammates) have to create a strategy on the fly. 

Furthermore, DRG is the only co-op shooter I know where 3d traversal is a REAL thing. Other games have ladders and stairs. DRG will let you drill tunnels, rig ziplines, and make climbing-holds. And don't worry, the bugs can climb walls... And remember that all of the terrain is destructible (the Engineer class can also shoot pancake-shaped platforms). You can remove environmental obstructions, make bunkers, and goofy trench networks. There is so much flexibility in how you approach objectives. I will say that on the higher levels DRG can get pretty movement-intensive (I think I've done more bunny-hopping on Deep Dives than in DOOM 2016, and scout gameplay is basically DOOM Eternal). 

There is also an amazing deal of flexibility with weapon customization. From the early game, you have access to an intuitive and impactful modding system. But once you reach the mid/late game you get these special upgrades that can radically change the functionality of your gear--- so much so that they may function like entirely different weapons. 

The enemy design and variety is very strong. Every critter has unique sounds, animations, weaknesses/resistances, and ways to ruin your day. The spawning is randomized at the start of every mission, so always expect different "specialist" enemies.

So is DRG for you? I think that other games have the capacity to add more content in terms of weapons and classes. But I think that DRG more than makes up for this with it's ability for players to overhaul their existing weapons and its incredible map-system. It's an entire order of magnitude more polished than anything else out there. And the community is the most supportive and least-toxic bunch of dwarves I've ever encountered.

If you want a melee system that's deeper than "weak standard attack, strong power-attack", more fine-tune load-out customization, a slightly more challenging endgame, and more visceral gore, then go to Darktide. 

And if you want massively overpowered weaponry, more explosions, a more arcade-y feel, and can't stand FPV, Helldivers 2 is for you. 

I will also say that Ghost Ship games is a far more responsible and less cash-hungry developer than Fatshark or Arrowhead. DRG has a battlepass, but it's entirely free and no items in it disappear forever. 

I hope this review has been helpful and that you are able to make a more informed decision about whether or not the dwarf life is for you

Rock and Stone!

One of my all-time favourite games. I've been playing on and off for over 3 years on multiple platforms, and it's still a blast.
Easy to pick up, nothing complicated, and no maze of menus to navigate. 
The gunplay is varied and fun, with satisfying feedback. You have 4 classes to choose from, each having their own set of main and secondary weapons, along with a choice of grenades, meaning most people will likely find a class and loadout that suits their style.

The art style and graphics really appeal to me, with the added bonus that this game runs incredibly well, even on my Steam Deck. 
The music, ambience and voice lines are all top tier. 

The multiplayer is excellent and where this game shines the most, although the matchmaking can sometimes be a little buggy. 
Missions can last anywhere from 10mins to an hour, depending on the mission type and the team skill level.
Most players will have all the guns unlocked after around 50 hours of playtime, and beyond that, there are endless cosmetics and weapon perks to unlock which will keep you playing for dozens or even hundreds of more hours.

My only negative is playing on Hazard 5.  This is where I found most of the insufferable players who hyperfocus on efficiency over fun.

If you're thinking of trying this out, I highly recommend.

Got gifted this game during Season 3, but i haven't really gotten into it until Season 4 rolled around. I missed out on a lot.

The game is simply good. The majority of players you encounter in the lobbies are really chill and usually have no problem with you messing something up. The gameplay loop is nice, there's no huge penalties for losing the mission, the only paid content is the game itself and the DLC armors and skins, which are purely cosmetic. 

The seasons have their own "season pass," which is free as well. AND, as of Season 5, you can simply go back to replay the old seasons if you haven't finished some or never played them. This also helped the developers to put the cosmetics from their perspective seasons back into these said seasons, thus lessening the loot bloat in the "cargo crates," "lost packs" and "core infusers" And as for loot, you never get double of the thing you already own (unless its a beard or a weapon skin for a separate class), which means that you're closer to getting what you want every time.

The game is primarily co-op, but it also lets you to play "solo" with a drone that follows you, shoots bugs and mines minerals that you point towards to. You can always disable the drone for the true solo experience if you're brave enough.

The developers, Ghost Ship Games, also deserve huge praise. Actually listening to the community and often interacting with them is such a welcome change in the sea of triple A bullcrap. They're nice people.

Cannot recommend this game enough. Once you get into the groove of things, it's real fun.

I have played this game for years now. Absolutely one of the best games I have ever played in my life. I have played thousands of games in my life. I started gaming when I was around 11 years old on an Atari 2600,then a commodore Vic 20, then a commodore 64 which I eventually had over 600 games for. I am 60 years old now and have been through many computers. My point being I have a massive amount of gaming experience and I am telling you this game makes my top 5 best games I have ever  played in my life. If you give this game a chance I believe it will become an addiction for you the way that it has become one for me. What do i say is giving it a chance? I say play till at least you make level 25 with at least one of the 4 possible characters, because thats when the game allows you to start getting over clocks for your weapons and also when can start doing deep dives. One of my favorite parts of the game is that you play co op and support one another as a team fighting against everything that is trying to kill all of you. As long as one person on the team is still up you can revive another team mate provided you dont go down yourself before you can revive them. The sound effects and music in game amp up the  excitement  and giddiness while playing. It feels really good if you can save the whole team and the mission with your skill as a player. Friendly fire is something you learn to deal with as your skill grows. I didnt start using plasma burster missles until I made level 1300 and something for fear of killing my team mates ,but I feel comfortable using them on a team now ,because I have developed the skill to use them without killing my team mates and they are beautiful to watch and extremely powerful against dreadnaughts in my opinion. What are dreadnaughts you ask? you will  have to play to find out. The hiveguard is the worst dreadnaught  by the way. Anyway this is a long winded and meandering review but I encourage any one that is interested to give this game a try. Its an amazing game even though they just stole all my 1403 levels , all my gold and all  my perks. Something happened to the game recently and I still support it even though I want my 500 plus barely bulbs back for buying beer.

I didn't fully understand this game when I first picked it up around its early access release. It sat forgotten in my library for a good year or two after that, gathering dust and honestly, I didn't even think about it. 

When I decided one day to try it out again I was shocked at why I didn't stick with the game the first time around. DRG has been like crack cocaine for me — the gameplay loop, weapons and gear customisation, enemy and mission variety — it has SO much content and SO much going on. 

The best thing by far about this game is its community though. I remember starting as a greenbeard and finding lobbies with veterans who patiently guided me and assisted me for hours on end. Now, after 900 hours I find myself returning the favour to newer players. It doesn't feel like a task or a chore, it brings genuine joy to help the community of a game that has helped me. 

Deep Rock Galactic is likely my favourite game of all time and I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a chill and friendly community and often chaotic missions full of adrenaline and pure fun.

You can drink beer.

I jumped into Deep Rock Galactic thinking “yeah this looks alright,” and came out shouting ROCK AND STONE like it’s a legally binding greeting.

This game is chaos in the best possible way. You and your friends drop into a cave, immediately get lost, accidentally split up, panic when bugs start pouring out of the walls, and somehow still make it out alive while laughing the whole time. It’s less “tactical mission” and more “dwarven survival comedy.”

The co-op is where it really shines. Every class actually feels useful, so instead of fighting over who gets to be the main character, you’re all just equally responsible for the inevitable disaster. And when things go wrong, they go spectacularly wrong.

And then there’s the bar. Honestly, half my playtime feels like it’s just spent in the Space Rig at the bar, ordering drinks, dancing like absolute idiots, and raising a beer for Karl like true dwarves.

ROCK AND STONE isn’t just a voice line at this point, it’s a lifestyle choice.

Verdict:
🍺 10/10 would mine again
🍺 10/10 would get lost again
🍺 FOR KARL

If you’ve got friends and a sense of humour, Deep Rock Galactic is an easy recommendation. If you don’t have friends… the game might help with that too.

If you ever played Minecraft and thought that it could use more bug killing and less building, this game might be for you.

If you've ever played Helldivers and wished you could have a side of mining with your bug-killing, this game might be for you.

Do you like a game that you can put down and pick back up with zero penalty? Then this game is for you.

Deep Rock Galactic is a game about dwarves in the far flung future doing what dwarves do best - digging for rare materials. The planet you're digging on, Hoxxes, is an environment that often tries to kill you as much as you mine it. There's a wide range of different missions to pick and choose, and often modifiers on them to spice it up. Each map is procedurally generated and this is to its benefit.

And the best part? There's no microtransactions. If you're feeling spicy and want to support, they have plenty of cosmetic items that you can purchase to support production, but its just that - cosmetics. If you want to play previous seasons passes (no paying for battlepasses here!) you can simply go back and just select them, and level them up the same way you would the current one.

There are a variety of weapons to choose from (and unlock from the assignments board once you've levelled one of your four classes enough) and each weapon has its own individual modifiers on it - and thats before you get into overclocks for the weapons.

There's also a variety of difficulty levels to challenge yourself and potential teammates. No team? No problem, you have a little robotic buddy to help you mine, kill bugs, and pick you up if you get put down by a nasty critter.

11/10 will always recommend purchase of this game to *anyone*.

ROCK AND STONE!

Deep Rock Galactic is what I would consider a near perfect video game. It has everything I love in games, all wrapped up into a single, chaotic package. Satisfying guns to shoot, rewarding grinding, fun movement mechanics, and masterful use of procedural generation that ensures every mission is fun and endlessly replayable.

Each of the characters are genuinely funny, full of character, and impossible not to love. The gameplay swings between moments of tense combat, and brief well-earned downtime effortlessly. And teamwork is heavily encouraged, but not required, and the game accommodating both is a testament to its brilliant design.

Then there's the community. I've played in open lobbies for years, and I can count every toxic encounter I've had on one hand. That's unheard of in modern gaming. Combine that with deep loadout customisation, theorycrafting, metagames and an atmosphere dripping with style, and you've truly made something special. The visual design is distinct and memorable, the soundtrack is incredible (Genuinely, never turn it down), and every session feels like a story worth telling. 

Dropping into a Haz5 cave feels like storming the beaches of Normandy. I love carving through an entire swarm using a mini-gun that's almost larger than the dwarf I'm playing as, or tossing grenades behind Doretta as she drills through a tunnel packed with bugs. I love playing with a driller and watching as they make a bunkie and turn a chokepoint into a glowing sludge pit of death. And I especially love those moments when I'm seconds away from boarding the drop pod, only for the 2nd gunner to go down 150 metres away, and suddenly the mission changes from escape to rescue, because [b] No Dwarf Gets Left Behind. [/b]

Deep Rock Galactic is packed with moments like this, and they are endlessly satisfying. It's a game that consistently delivers where so many others can't. For years, whenever other games have disappointed me, I've always been able to rely on DRG to just be a genuinely fun game for me to go back to. It's been S+ tier since day one, and only ever gets better.

Ghost Ship deserves far more recognition than they get. They've built one of the most consistently excellent, community driven and lovingly maintained games in the industry. If Team Fortress 2 hadn't already stolen my heart long ago, Deep Rock Galactic would easily take the number 1 spot.

Rock and Stone to the Bone.

I genuinely love Deep Rock Galactic. I’ve put hundreds of hours into it, bought cosmetics, convinced friends to play it, and defended the game for years because it used to feel like one of the few co-op games made by developers who actually cared.

Instead of properly supporting the game that built the community, the studio seems more interested in chasing trends with spin-offs like Survivor — which is basically “Vampire Survivors but with dwarves” — and now Rogue Core, which feels like another attempt to turn DRG into a roguelite instead of improving the original game people actually fell in love with.

Meanwhile the base game barely gets meaningful updates anymore. Not even regular balance tweaks, quality-of-life passes, weapon reworks, bugfixes, or hotfixes at the pace you’d expect from a live-service co-op game this popular. There are bugs and issues that sit around forever while development focus clearly goes elsewhere.

And before people spam “the game already has enough content” — that’s not the point. The point is that the original DRG became successful because of the gameplay loop, teamwork, and constant support. Now it feels like that support has slowed to a crawl while the brand gets stretched into side projects.

I’m not even saying Rogue Core or Survivor are terrible games. I’m saying it sucks watching the original game slowly lose momentum while the developers move on to copy-and-paste trend chasing.

DRG deserved better long-term support than this.

Killing bugs feels satisfying, the objectives on most missions allow for a fair amount of player autonomy so you don't need to play too close to your team all the time. There's a lot to like about the game.

Why the negative review, then? Unfortunately, developers of the game recently decided to practically abandon the game in favour of a rogue-lite spinoff called Rogue Core (for those unfamiliar, rogue-lites are a genre of early access ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ classified as such because they include some form of randomness and brainless stat-multiplication, named after Rogue because that game had randomness in the form of procedural generation... and uh... yeah that's all), leaving this game to an outsource development team that then released the worst seasonal update the game has ever seen, that being season 6. Don't get me wrong, the last few seasons before season 6 had been immense ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ too - Deep Scan lags the hell out of your game as it progresses, likely due to a memory leak, and the game's netcode simply can't handle the sheer amount of terrain destroyed as the mission closes, adding network lag on top of even worse framerates. One of the newest enemies added before season 6, the Corespawn Crawler, is a bullet sponge with a weakpoint the size of a peanut (which it may decide to not even expose, depending on the horoscope) that can also leap at you like a coyote and hit you even if you're running straight away from it, all while spawning in considerable numbers, prompting most teams to not even attempt the event that spawns it, UNLESS... there is a gunner on the team, who can just throw a zipline down for his entire team to sit on, at which point the event becomes a complete joke as Crawlers can no longer reach you. Amazing game design.

But, as I said, all of this pales in comparison to the monumental pile of ♥♥♥♥ that season 6 is - the single smallest seasonal content update the game has seen, where all that was added was a drab (but admittedly atmospheric) biome and two new enemies exclusive to said biome - a scarab with hit detection so inconsistent that you might as well not bother dodging or reading its movement, and a ground-leech that can grab you from so far away that you might think the game bears you a personal grudge. Oh, and also a mission type that transforms your frames per second into seconds per frame every time you complete an objective, again due to the sheer amount of terrain being updated. And of course, to slap a band-aid on the microscopic amount of content the season added, the seasonal modifiers for season 6 just regurgitate these scarabs and ground-leeches into biomes outside of the one newly added in season 6.

Speaking of content regurgitation, did I mention that the last two updates the game has gotten are 1. an event that forces even more of those God-awful Corespawn Crawlers upon you and 2. a shill update with an assignment rewarding players with the pickaxe skin from Rogue Core just to get more eyes on their upcoming wire coat hanger abortion of a video game?

Since I'm on the topic of Rogue Core, I'll also briefly mention that I played its closed beta before the game's launch, and that it's is flawed on a fundamental level. It strips away exactly what made DRG fun - autonomy and sparse teamplay - and replaces it with a slow, grating gameplay loop with frustrating teamplay. I heard from someone closer to the game's community than I am that DRG itself was initially supposed to be a rogue-lite like how Rogue Core is now, and if that has any truth to it, I'm very glad it didn't turn out a rogue-lite and suspect that the idea was dropped because it was retarded in the first place. Assuming that this claim is true and not just an excuse to jump on the latest normie bandwagon, of course.

Lastly, I'll touch on my more minor grievances with this game. The devs aren't very receptive to community feedback, or atleast very weakly receptive to it. It seems like GSG is sometimes heading in the right direction like with the recent (well, 'recent' - it was something like three years ago) Subata rework, but at this point I have little hope for any more quality reworks or rebalances. This isn't for lack of anything to change, by the way - the perk system has been begging for a rework for ages and some weapon choices for classes are so bad that it's a headache to use them. Some enemies like Stingtails are buggy and launch you way too far when they connect, and sometimes forgo their attack warning sound entirely. Newly added stalkers are obnoxiously loud and barely visible even under the best lighting conditions, which makes them frustrating to locate unless you have an aoe weapon. Despite being a co-op team-based game, you don't have many ways to coordinate with your team. You can shoot the bugs that are chasing your friends, of course, but you don't have any way to know what build your teammates are using without a third-party mod, which can lead to you bringing a conflicting build to the mission. Best example is driller - one of his primary weapons is a flamethrower, another is a cryo cannon. If you want to join a mission as driller when the lobby already has a driller, you're forced to gamble and hope you don't drop in with a build that will cuck your counterpart's playstyle.

Oh, and please, for the sake of your own sanity, if you take away one thing from this review, let it be this. Limit your interactions with this game's community as much as possible. Aside from the usual colourful suspects present everywhere in the game's discord, reddit, mod.io, forums, etc, even more unassuming players can't seem to help but be caught up in this sort of larper's herd mentality where they MUST ping gold chunks or mushrooms while sitting in one place for ages. If one time is funny and two times is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying, hearing 'we're rich' six million times could turn a saint into Adolf Hitler. Thankfully, this is only a problem on lower difficulties, you'd be hard pressed to find anyone who stalls the game to deepthroat a yellow boulder on haz5+ or even haz5. If you do find such an anomalous ♥♥♥♥♥♥, take the rock from his hands, deposit it, and tell him that you'd prefer to be banned instead of kicked if he's too uppity. Problem solved. To give praise where it is due, the lassaiz-faire lobby browser model is actually quite nice, and prevents the game's colourful horde community from interfering with the game itself. The most you can do to a player you dislike is ban him if you're the lobby host, or choose not to play with him and disconnect if you're not. If there is a way to report a player to have him banned from all lobbies permanently, I have not found it in almost 2000 hours of play.

In short, I love this game. Which is exactly why I must give it a harsh review when it's being unfairly neglected by its own developers. Glazediver-tier shills will tell you there's nothing wrong with the game and that you must rock and stone, live in ze bunker and eat ze gold, but these are the same people that would shove a plate full of ♥♥♥♥ in their mouths if they were allowed to laserpoint it for half an hour first. I sincerely doubt Ghost Ship Games is actively malicious and hates the product of their own love and labour, more likely is that they think they can get away with more than they actually can thanks to misleading shills who love talking about the game more than actually playing it. If someone had told me that a resource extraction simulator with FPS elements would be a successful combination, I would have shaken my head in disbelief. My presence as a skeptic and an ignoramus is proven by the fact that I have spent multiple hours playing this strange combination which now captivates me.

🎮Although Deep Rock Galactic is not the newest title, having premiered in 2k20, I hadn't had the opportunity to play it until couple of years later. I was unable to play DRG until two years after its release because I was unaware of the game until that time. The Danish studio Ghost Ship Games has maintained the game's presence in public awareness by regularly releasing it on new gaming platforms.

But to the point. The game lets players control dwarf miners who work for the titular corporation on a planet called Hoxxes IV. The developers chose to omit a story because they believed it would not benefit this type of gameplay and I fully support their decision. The mission requires players to collect all available ore while staying alive in hazardous underground environments which contain deadly monsters.

The study area for our research remains restricted to our operational base which consists of a spacecraft and its associated mission sites. The base allows us to change our character's appearance and skills while we can upgrade our drone system and use the facility to break barrels and consume beer.
We use our earned income to purchase both equipment and cosmetic features at this location. The locations consist of procedurally generated caves which vary in size and provide different tasks and experiences that include fighting enemies and collecting resources and searching for monster eggs. The building design includes corridor paths which enable various activities to search for minerals and determine their paths back to base. The digital GPS system presented my main mapping challenge because I could not understand its functions at first which led me to disable its use. The laser pointer and the Bosco bot provided essential assistance to me during my work.

We encounter swarms of monsters during every exploration we conduct. The developers created characters who function as more than simple targets for players to eliminate. The spider-like monsters create challenges that our team needs to handle. The different types of armor provide various levels of protection while their special abilities and specific damage types remaining impervious to harm. The Miner's Handbook which exists on our spaceship contains all necessary information to defeat our enemies.

DRG is a game designed for co-op. Let's not kid ourselves. Solo gaming becomes acceptable until players reach their first limit. The task becomes more difficult as we advance through the forest and into the caves. The game provides excellent content which players should experience together with their friends. The game allows players to achieve more while their overall enjoyment of the game experience increases.
I previously played this game alone, but now with friends and sometimes random users joining the session, greatly improved the gameplay for me.
The bot Bosco provides essential assistance during our mission gameplay when we play without other people. The robot can shoot at enemies while it can also illuminate specific objects and extract minerals which are beyond our reach. The initial resources prove insufficient for success during the game's final stages. The dwarven miners work as a group only when players choose to join them, yet solitary players will not survive because of this.

I really like the fact that you can change your dwarf class at any time (except during missions, of course).
We have the Driller, who burns his enemies with a flamethrower and digs through the terrain with drilling gloves.
The Engineer, who creates turrets and platforms,
Gunner, who has a minigun and a zipline,
And the Scout, who provides support to the team.
The first two of these dwarves are my favorites. The characters in this game maintain strong harmony with each other which becomes essential for gameplay progression through the later stages.

The mission is the mission, but we can also do some sightseeing!
The graphics of DRG display bright colors which create a slightly cartoonish appearance. The game reminded me of Borderlands and Minecraft because of its use of angular multi-colored design elements. The caves, in particular, deserve attention because their different plant life and color patterns and surface materials create unique displays. The lighting is also impressive. Since it's dark everywhere we have to use flares to create light that helps us see and navigate the space. The lighting effects are truly top-notch.

The production does not display any visual excellence because it contains only basic visual elements. The game maintains perfect performance because it runs at sixty frames per second without any interruptions. I played the game without experiencing any technical difficulties or visual errors. This is what matters when playing online, especially when time is of the essence.

I have no additional comments about the music content. The music tracks for this project create an appropriate atmosphere which matches the visual content but they do not create lasting impressions. Our current situation determines which musical tones we will hear between walking through Egyptian darkness and facing an attack from mutated insect swarms. The dwarves' dialogues and comments during various actions are great. My favorite line from the movie is "I can do this all day" because it instantly brought Captain America to my mind.

TL;DR: The built-in mod support is bad, their handling of the modding scene is limiting for no good reason and hostile towards people who want to make the game better, recent regional price increases, and they are now unwilling to accept the feedback that has gotten them to where they are now.

[h1]Modding[/h1]

The built-in modding support is laughably bad. I don't know how anyone who designed it would look at it, go, "Yup, this is something I would use", and then ship it. A 50 mod cap and general instability across the board - I have genuinely had mods turn off on me with no discernible pattern for no reason - means that you're better off using a third party solution (Mint, in this case). It would genuinely be better and less confusing to remove the built-in mod support and let the community do it. Most games do this, and it works! It's less development effort wasted on pointless things, and less confusion for new players who might not understand why things aren't working or why there are pointless restrictions that don't need to be there. I suspect the only reason we have a built-in mod manager is because GSG had a business deal with mod.io, which is not a player-friendly reason, but don't quote me on that because that's just a theory.

Regardless, my modding-related issues go beyond the built-in mod manager and go more into community moderation and handling of the game's modding scene.

Recently, when I got sucked back into playing the game, I joined the Discord server to ask how Nitra generation in caves worked. Did it work like in RoR2 where chests and other interactables are generated based on a credit balance assigned by the stage? The DRG wiki goes into some depth on how bugs are spawned in announced swarms, but the documentation on Nitra generation left a lot to be desired, which pales in comparison to the RoR2 wiki's extensive documentation on its director system. I found that odd, because the two games have been out for maybe about the same time.

Perhaps that was a sign of things to come, because I asked, and I was quickly met with someone saying, "I can't share that here, I'll send you a friend request" (paraphrased). Coming from RoR2 and other decompilation and modding heavy communities, this struck me as odd. (For the deeply curious, you can find this exchange on the official DRG Discord server [url=https://discord.com/channels/257785731072786435/257785731072786435/1501406799587180695]here[/url].

It's fairly clear that, despite DRG being a peer-to-peer online game with a large community backing (like RoR2), without which this game would not have continued to get support, GSG has displayed animosity, or at least a lack of care, towards mod developers on multiple occasions. If you look at the top mods list on mod.io for more than two seconds, you'll find mods like Build Inspector, whose descriptions describe being punished for releasing alternatives to popular mods, the authors of which were doing [i]genuinely user-unfriendly things[/i], and then getting extremely unhelpful responses from GSG. It's the same ♥♥♥♥ you see in real life where people doing things that help the community are reprimanded, while hostile folks are left to do whatever they want scot-free because I dunno they're privileged or something.

What if I got into modding DRG? Would I be treated with the same hostility that AssemblyStorm and other mod creators faced? I have no way of knowing, and I'm not interested in finding out, so I don't plan on making mods for this game on mod.io. Playing into GSG's modding ecosystem would do nothing positive for me.

Taking microscopic ♥♥♥♥♥ on the community that made your game what it is, is not the answer. Obviously. So don't do that.

[h1]Regional pricing increase for DRG and its DLCs[/h1]

A couple of months ago, the price of DRG and its Packs were increased in some currencies.

This is in direct contrast to Rogue Core's pricing, which I'm aware is cheaper than DRG after accounting for inflation.

Most likely, GSG or Coffee Stain Publishing changed the pricing to fit the [url=https://steamdb.info/blog/valve-price-matrix-2026-update/]updated regional pricing settings[/url]. I'm not sure why they would choose the setting that [i]increased[/i] pricing for a lot of people. You can come to your own conclusion here, but I'm not personally a fan.

[h1]"We want feedback!" said the company who doesn't want feedback[/h1]

I wasn't around when Core Spawn were first added to DRG in Season 5, but it seems to me like a lot of people don't like it. I'm probably a part of this camp - they don't really fit the game that well and were only really added to tie into Rogue Core. So, with most people not liking it, I find it interesting that the response to that was to add more Core Spawn in the form of a new mutator in Season 6, where Core Spawn will [i]immediately[/i] spawn, there is irregular terrain, and the only way to stop the Core Spawn from spawning is to do the mutator that you are already now required to do anyway.

I'm aware S6 was made by a different developer, but I imagine GSG still had a say in whether the final feature was okay, and GSG were the ones that made the original Core Spawn event. So GSG most likely agrees that the answer to people not liking a feature, should be to add [i]more[/i] of that disliked feature while simultaneously exacerbating the things they didn't like about it.

...It goes without saying that this is not how feedback should work. If I were working on this, and I saw that most of my playerbase did not like a thing I added, I would have reworked or removed it. But by Karl, GSG has a vision and they're dead set on it! Even if nobody likes it! It's a stark contrast from what long-time players have been saying about DRG's early days, and that makes me even more confused; it's like GSG didn't learn their lesson from Early Access at all and are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around with whatever [i]they[/i] want to do, with no regard for what their [i]community[/i] wants.

I've also seen sentiment from Rogue Core closed alpha players that their feedback went unheard. I'm not confident enough in what I've seen to say anything definitive about it, but it is a thing. And considering how Core Spawn was handled, I would not be surprised if it was true, nor if it had happened before while I wasn't playing.

Finally - can you fix the netcode that you know has been broken for years, so I stop disconnecting every match??
